rows.description: A toddler scribbles, smears paint or squashes clay for the sensory joy of making marks. Early marks show exploration and motor growth, not representational meaning, so praising effort beats asking what it is.
A school-age child builds a model, folds origami or makes a card, showing pride, patience and care for the recipient. Specific comments on the work support motivation better than general flattery.
A young adult shapes film, graphic design or architecture to communicate a viewpoint or emotion to strangers. Audiences read work through their own experience, so intent and reception can differ.

rows.subtype: Restless boredom on a long afternoon [Actor]
rows.description: A child sighs "I am bored" through a holiday afternoon, then after a while invents a game; boredom is often the doorway to imagination when nobody hurries to fill it.

rows.subtype: Life feels flat after a big goal is reached [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult who got into their dream college finds themselves oddly hollow; a long-chased goal removed the direction it gave, leaving a quiet weariness.
A young professional moves through the same commute and tasks, not sad but grey and tired of the sameness, and drifts toward numbing habits instead of change.

rows.subtype: One sweet now, not two later [Actor]
rows.description: A young child cannot wait for a bigger treat and grabs the smaller one at once. The future is hard to picture and the present is loud.
A teenager prefers an hour of gaming now over a better grade in months. Distant benefits feel weak while immediate pleasure feels vivid.
A student spends his stipend at once, knowing he will want the savings later. He plans to be disciplined next month, and next month repeats the choice.
A child sees that a classmate walks far to school while they arrive by car, or that some friends have a quiet place to study. They start to ask why, and may feel guilty, curious or defensive.
A teenager told they had it easier feels attacked, and answers "but I worked hard". Hard work and unearned advantage can both be true, and the second does not cancel the first.

rows.subtype: Toddler wound up by fast screens [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler who watches fast, bright videos before bed may be more wired, cranky and slow to sleep. Quiet play, books and a screen-free wind-down help the small brain settle.

A teenager scrolling in bed feels one more video is harmless, but sleep is delayed and mood the next day drops. Fear of missing out and bright light both keep the mind alert long after tiredness sets in.

rows.subtype: Working screens late into the night [Actor]
rows.description: A professional answering messages and emails late finds the mind still buzzing at bedtime and wakes unrested. Clear work boundaries and a screen-free half hour before sleep help the brain shift gears.
A new graduate discovers that the real rules of the office, such as who to copy on emails and when to speak, are unwritten. They watch closely and feel anxious about missteps.
An ambitious employee builds alliances and shapes impressions to rise. Some networking is normal, and it turns harmful when it involves undermining others or hiding facts.
